description: ฅ is an obsolete Thai consonant letter. In its normal initial position, it represents the aspirated /kʰ/ sound, like the k in English “key” or “cat” with a noticeable puff of air. In some loanword spellings, such as เวอร์, the same visible sequence is part of a different vowel spelling and is pronounced /wɤː/.
description: Usually, เว is pronounced /weː/: like the beginning of English “way,” but with a steady, slightly longer vowel and no English-style diphthong. The ว is a /w/ sound. In some transliterated loanwords, especially เวอร์ (“over”), it is pronounced /wɤː/, somewhat like the vowel in “bird” without the strong English r.

thoughts: The basic เก spelling is quite easy for English speakers because its vowel resembles the vowel in “say.” The main unfamiliar feature is that Thai ก is unaspirated, so it sounds closer to the k in “skill” than the strongly puffed k in “key.” The sequence can also be part of larger vowel combinations, so its exact sound depends on the letters and tone marks that follow it.
description: เก normally represents ก followed by the long vowel /eː/: approximately the vowel in English “say,” but with a clean, unaspirated /k/ sound. The vowel sign เ is written before ก but pronounced after it. When additional vowel letters or tone marks follow, the combination can change—for example, เก้า is /kâo/ (“kao”), and เกี๊ยว begins /kiaw/.

thoughts: ซร is an uncommon Thai consonant sequence. In some words or pronunciations, the cluster may be simplified toward /s/.

thoughts: This is a complete Thai spelling sequence rather than just one sound. It is pronounced /sàʔ/ as the independent word “vowel,” but often /sà/ at the beginning of compounds. The short vowel and optional glottal stop are somewhat unfamiliar to English speakers.
description: The sequence สระ is usually pronounced like Thai *sà*, approximately “suh” with a short, low falling tone. In compounds such as สระน้ำ, the same sequence is commonly an open syllable /sà/ without a clearly audible final stop. The ร is not pronounced as a separate r sound here.
